CweFindings.Name: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
CweFindings.Description: The product allows the upload or transfer of dangerous file types that are automatically processed within its environment.
CweFindings.Explanation: HomeController.uploadPhotos (lines 55-69) accepts multipart uploads from authenticated callers. PhotoServiceImpl.uploadPhoto trusts caller-supplied Content-Type at lines 87-94, derives an unrestricted extension at lines 112-115 and 243-248, and processes bytes with ImageIO at lines 124-137. An absent ImageReader at lines 131-149 or a non-IO parsing failure at lines 155-158 does not reject the upload: arbitrary non-image content labeled as an allowed image type is persisted at lines 160-174. PhotoFileController.servePhoto returns those original bytes at lines 58-83 with the supplied MIME type. This confirms missing actual-type validation and acceptance of disguised non-image content; server-side execution and browser execution of the binary content were not established, and authentication limits the upload actor.

CweFindings.Name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
CweFindings.Description: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input before it is placed in output that is used as a web page that is served to other users.
CweFindings.Explanation: PhotoServiceImpl.uploadPhoto stores the original multipart filename at lines 160-168 and HomeController.uploadPhotos returns it unescaped as JSON at lines 75-83. upload.js createPhotoCard inserts that filename directly into HTML attributes and element content at lines 181-189; displayNewPhotos passes the string to insertAdjacentHTML at lines 155-157. A crafted filename can break out of the HTML context and run script in the uploader browser. The independent showErrors sink at lines 215-218 also inserts client-controlled filenames from lines 71-83 or server failure data from lines 118-120 into innerHTML. Upload success requires authentication; this is confirmed DOM injection in upload feedback, not a claim that escaped server-rendered gallery templates execute stored markup for every viewer.

CweFindings.Name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
CweFindings.Description: The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.
CweFindings.Explanation: create-user.sh takes APP_USER from the environment at lines 7-13, uppercases it without SQL escaping at line 19, and expands it into an unquoted here-document sent to privileged sqlplus at lines 22-45. The username is directly embedded inside a SQL string literal in the SELECT at line 27 and dynamic DDL at lines 30-35. A single quote and SQL syntax in this upstream configuration can terminate the literal and modify the PL/SQL block. This is an initialization/configuration trust-boundary issue requiring influence over startup environment, not remotely supplied HTTP input; Spring Data repository queries use bound parameters instead.

CweFindings.Name: Unchecked Input for Loop Condition
CweFindings.Description: The product does not properly check inputs that are used for loop conditions, potentially leading to a denial of service or other consequences because of excessive looping.
CweFindings.Explanation: HomeController.uploadPhotos checks only null/empty at lines 62-66, then iterates every attacker-supplied multipart item at lines 68-90, invoking image parsing and database writes per item. The configured app.file-upload.max-files-per-upload=10 at application.properties:30 is never injected or enforced. PhotoServiceImpl validates each file size at lines 96-109 but not collection count. An authenticated caller can submit many small nonempty parts to force disproportionate looping, image probing and persistence operations. The 50 MB request limit and servlet parser limits constrain requests but do not enforce the intended 10-file workload bound; this is not a claim of literally unlimited request bytes.

CweFindings.Name: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value
CweFindings.Description: The product allocates memory based on an untrusted, large size value, but it does not ensure that the size is within expected limits, allowing arbitrary amounts of memory to be allocated.
CweFindings.Explanation: PhotoRepository.findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc selects every row including PHOTO_DATA without pagination at lines 22-27. PhotoServiceImpl.getAllPhotos materializes that result at lines 55-57, and the public HomeController.index invokes it at lines 37-41. Photo.photoData is a byte[] @Lob at lines 39-41 with no lazy fetch declaration, so the growing uploaded corpus is loaded into heap for a gallery metadata request. Repeated permitted uploads control the aggregate number and size of these allocations; the per-file 10 MB limit does not bound the total result. The configured runtime heap is 512 MB at Dockerfile:28. A sufficiently large corpus can exhaust memory on ordinary unauthenticated gallery reads. This is aggregate database-result allocation, not an unchecked individual multipart byte length; no runtime exhaustion test was performed.

CweFindings.Name: Insufficient Logging
CweFindings.Description: When a security-critical event occurs, the product either does not record the event or omits important details about the event when logging it.
CweFindings.Explanation: SecurityConfig.securityFilterChain requires authentication for upload/delete at lines 54-60, making these attributable security-sensitive mutations. PhotoServiceImpl.uploadPhoto records successful uploads with only filename and photo ID at lines 179-180; deletePhoto records only photo ID at line 212, and DetailController.deletePhoto logs only the ID at line 69. These recorded mutation events omit the authenticated principal and originating client, and none of these classes provides audit-context enrichment or an authentication-event listener. Consequently the application-level mutation log cannot attribute changes to a requester or correlate attempts reliably. Framework, reverse-proxy or deployment-specific audit sinks may add coverage, but none is configured in the inspected production files and runtime logging was not observed.
